newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW - Australian coal profits vanishing.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW - Australian coal profits vanishing.

text.p: Australian coal industry profits are disappearing in a squeeze between disappointing prices for exports to Japan in 1997/98 and currency problems.

Profits in 1995/96 to June 30 of about A$2.61 a tonne, on paper, would be fully absorbed by semi-soft coking coal price cuts of between A$2.50 and A$3.80 a tonne for Japanese fiscal year 1997/98 starting April 1, The chairman of the New South Wales Minerals Council, Terry O'Reilly, said in an interview.

The comments by O'Reilly, also managing director of Coal and Allied Industries Ltd, come as Australian steaming coal producers settle 1997/98 prices with Japan at meetings in Cairns, northern Queensland, capping off a disappointing negotiating round for Australian coal exporters.

"With the prospects we have in 1997, if we don't do anything different ... profitability will disappear," he said. "Be absolutely sure that a strong Australian dollar and a lower U.S. dollar price means a huge amount of pressure," he said.

With real coal prices in U.S. dollar terms in a long-term decline, 1997 presented producers with a survival requirement of productivity improvements year-in and year-out for both capital and labour, O'Reilly said.
An industry survey by the New South Wales Minerals Council and accounting firm Coopers and Lybrand showed the state's coal industry overall returned just 8.8 percent on funds in 1995/96.
The profitability impact of the 1997 crunch industry-wide would depend on how well-hedged different companies were at different exchange rates, O'Reilly said.
O'Reilly bases his calculations on semi-soft coking coal price cuts of US$2.00-$3.00 a tonne for 1997/98, with conversions at the current exchange rate of 78 U.S. cents.
Hard coking coal producers secured only average rollover prices for 1997/98, while steaming coal producers this week settled for a price cut of US$2.60-$2.70 a tonne.
An Australian dollar recovery from presently weaker levels would produce an even greater impact on Australian exporters, whose sales to Japan are set in U.S. dollars, he said.
But the stronger Australian dollar in the first half of 1996/97, an average 79 U.S. cents against 76.3 cents in 1995/96 and 69.2 cents in 1993/94, had pressured profits, he said.

Despite the industry dimmer prospects, companies in the Coopers and Lybrand survey indicated they planned to spend A$651 million on new and existing projects this financial year, compared with A$530 million last financial year.
Much of this was on-going capital re-injection.
But O'Reilly said he was not a pessimist on Australian coal, nor does he blame the Japanese for the industry's plight.
The Australian industry, particularly in steaming coal, had reached six to seven percent growth a year for the past seven or eight years and was forecast to continue at that rate, he said.
"That's what causes the optimism on the part of investors to some degree ... how well you can get your position on the cost curve to get a rate of return..."
This year's flat prices were not held down by Japanese buyers but reflected international supply/demand.
Over-supply resulted from 1995 and 1996 displacement of Australian tonnages from Europe by U.S. and South African coal, he said. This produced over-supply and more spot deals.
While there was a little excess in supply in thermal coal, demand was lumpy as new power stations came on stream while supply was lumpy as mines came on stream, he said.
"It's still Australia's largest export, it's still one of the few commodities (with) significant growth potential world-wide. Energy demand (in) nearby neighbours is Large."
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
